title: Using model routing to lower inference costs
summary: Running frontier models for coding and other purposes can be very expensive, but also, sometimes, very effective. It’s tempting to use smaller or older models instead of frontier models because they’re cheaper, although they may not work as well. The ideal model for any given task tends to depend on the complexity of the task. Picking the most appropriate model automatically based on the request and the context is called model routing. How model routing works There are several ways of implementing model routing. In general, model routing depends on the pool of available models, the criteria used for selecting a model, and the objective that the router is trying to optimize. Different vendors offer different implementations of this scheme. Databricks’ Unity Gateway has (in beta) Smart Routing for Codex or Claude Code. Smart Routing automatically selects the lowest-cost model capable of handling each task, so developers do not need to choose a model for every request. Microsoft’s model router , a trained language model, analyzes your prompts in real time based on complexity, reasoning, task type, and other attributes. It does not store your prompts. It routes only to eligible models based on your access and deployment types, honoring data zone boundaries. You can choose balanced mode, cost mode, or quality mode. Not Diamond Code uses a lightweight local proxy that computes the derived metadata needed for routing to evaluate the broader session, including expected downstream work and cache state, and select the model and reasoning effort that optimize expected quality and total session cost. It uses more capable models when they are likely to improve the outcome or finish in fewer steps, and more cost-efficient models when additional intelligence is unlikely to add value. NVIDIA’s NeMo Switchyard has an array of routing algorithms that it can use. title: How AI is changing software pricing
summary: In 2026, the AI monetization conversation has shifted quickly from one concern to the next. Early in the year, fears that AI agents would erode software seats helped trigger a selloff of software stocks dubbed the “SaaSpocalypse.” Since then, attention has turned to a different disruption, as AI leaders including Anthropic , OpenAI, and GitHub lean heavily on usage-based pricing to better align revenue with the cost of delivering AI. It would be easy to conclude that software monetization is shifting wholesale from seats and subscriptions to tokens, credits, and consumption. But look across a broader cross-section of the software industry, and a different picture emerges. Most software companies aren’t AI-native businesses designing pricing from scratch. They have existing products, customers, contracts, and pricing structures. They’re adding AI to portfolios that may already span dozens of products and multiple monetization models. And they have to balance the economics of AI with something customers still value enormously: predictability. That tension came through clearly in our new Revenera Monetization Monitor: Software and AI Pricing Models and Strategies 2027 report of 415 product and technology leaders at established software producers and intelligent device manufacturers. Nearly all are adding AI capabilities to at least some products. The way they’re monetizing those capabilities, though, is considerably more pragmatic than the headlines might suggest. AI features are widespread, but adoption is lagging AI capabilities have gone mainstream. The share of software producers incorporating AI into their products jumped from 80% last year to 96% today. Getting AI into the product, however, is only the first step. The widespread use of chatbots can create the impression that everyone is using AI. title: Eight reasons coding agents are better than software developers
summary: I can’t stop anthropomorphizing my coding agent. I use both Claude Code and Cursor , and whenever I talk about these tools, I always refer to them as “he”, as in “He found and fixed a bug I never even realized existed.” The reason for this is probably obvious. I deal with my coding agent as if he were a colleague on the other end of a chat window. He writes great code and explains everything clearly. And frankly, it’s gotten to the point where he is a better software developer than any human developer could possibly be. So in the spirit of all great listicles, here are eight reasons that coding agents are better software developers than we are. Coding agents are tireless We all get tired. We all sleep badly. Your coding agent never does. He is always ready, always perky, and always 100% on the job. He codes just as well at 4:45 pm on a Friday as he does at 8:45 am Monday morning. He will work without stopping until he solves the problem at hand. He is available 24/7/365. And he never hangs around the break room kibitzing. Coding agents are faster He types faster than you. He reads code faster than you. He thinks faster than you. There probably isn’t anything he does slower than you. Coding agents have no ego A coding agent can’t get his feelings hurt when you push back on what he is doing (well, not yet, anyway). He doesn’t argue with you, though maybe he should. He is always open to suggestions, and he doesn’t care who has a good idea. He will gladly rename 400 files or upgrade all your dependencies without a peep of complaint. Coding agents know every programming language, stack, and framework Sure, you may have spent years becoming an expert at three or four languages, and you can work fluently in a few of the best frameworks. But you’ll never be an expert in all of them. Claude Code is. And he’ll learn new languages, stacks, and frameworks faster than you will too.
